newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends firmer as Swiss franc losses pile up.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends firmer as Swiss franc losses pile up.

text.p: The dollar ended mostly higher in an abbreviated session Friday, scoring a three-year high against the Swiss franc and briefly hitting a fresh four-year peak vs. the Japanese yen.
But continuing reports that Japanese monetary authorities had acted to support the yen offset the dollar's steady gains vs. European currencies.
U.S. bond and currency markets ended early in observance of the Presidents Day holiday on Monday.

During Asian trading the dollar peaked at 124.82 yen, a level not seen since February 1992, but quickly retreated after word spread on trading floors that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) had expressed interest in selling dollars at 125 yen.
A day earlier many traders in London claimed to have seen the Bank of England buying yen for the Bank of Japan.
"I'm pretty sure the BOJ was checking rates," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co. in New York. "I don't know if it was just simply intended to spook the market."

Investors have watched carefully for central bank market intervention since last Saturday's meeting of economic officials of the Group of Seven industrialised nations ended with statements calling for an end to the dollar's rich rally.
Recent reports have cited 1.70 German marks and 125 yen as the target rates of G7 leaders and the dollar has failed to rise past those levels in recent sessions.
"I'd say the G7 seems to have accomplished what they want," said Frank Pusateri, corporate foreign exchange vice president at Mellon Bank in Boston. "They have stability around these levels."
The dollar ended at 1.6880 marks, up from 1.6830 late Thursday, and at 124.33 yen vs. 124.25.
The dollar rose to 1.4630 Swiss francs from 1.4545, but fell to Canadian $1.3505 from C$1.3514. The British pound fell to $1.6200 from $1.6240.
Persistent weakness in the Swiss economy, coupled with historically low official interest rates, continue to erode the value of the franc and lift the dollar in Europe, dealers said.
Swiss officials have repeatedly expressed a desire to see the franc weaken further, which would make Swiss exports less expensive and boost Switzerland's anaemic economy.
A pair of economic releases pushed the dollar lower in early New York trading, dealers said.
The Labour Department reported producer prices fell 0.3 percent in January, and the Federal Reserve said industrial output failed to rise last month.
"That does signal that the Federal Reserve is less likely to have to raise rates," said Brian McCarthy, market analyst at Ruesch International.
Low inflation and moderating U.S. economic growth would reduce current pressure for higher domestic interest rates, making U.S. investments and the dollar less attractive.
